Combines synthetic recovery experiments, including assumption violations and three-run variability, with broad CLIP evaluations across datasets, backbones, and shot counts.
The proposed post-processing is simple and reports useful downstream gains; for example, PCA plus FastICA improves ViT-B/16 two-shot average target accuracy from 32.51% to 37.13%.

Its required almost-sure equality between paired embeddings also forces constant representations under the full-support noisy coupling in Eq. (4), contradicting its uniform-output condition. This invalidates the shared-encoder and nuisance-removal argument used by both main identifiability theorems.

The convex-body proof has an additional substantive error. Equation (43) treats p(z_t) as exactly uniform, although Lemma 4.2 only establishes a limiting claim as lambda approaches zero. At finite lambda, boundary-dependent normalization generally produces a nonuniform marginal, invalidating the stated cross-entropy reduction. Appendix K regresses learned representations on ground-truth latents; this R-squared can be perfect for a rank-deficient linear representation that discards latent factors. Held-out prediction in the reverse direction and rank checks are needed. On real data, selected CelebA traversals and downstream accuracy improvements cannot establish identifiability, and quantitative disentanglement measurements are absent.

The causal contribution and novelty are overstated. An undirected dependency between latent variables does not by itself establish causal semantics or demonstrate an advance beyond DAG-based modeling. Reproducibility and reporting need improvement. Real-data results lack uncertainty across runs, and the data used to fit PCA/FastICA and select component counts are insufficiently specified. The experiments cover synthetic recovery, distributional assumption violations, CelebA traversals, four CLIP encoders, ImageNet distribution shifts, and few-shot adaptation across 11 datasets.

The lightweight postprocessing reports meaningful improvements. For example, PCA plus FastICA raises ViT-B/16 two-shot ImageNet accuracy from 44.97% to 46.57% and average target-domain accuracy from 32.51% to 37.13%.

Moreover, its required equality h_x(z_x)=h_t(z_t) almost surely forces constant representations under the finite-concentration vMF model, whose joint density has full support. This contradicts the simultaneous uniformity requirement. Both Theorems 4.1 and 4.3 depend on this argument, leaving the principal guarantees unestablished.

The convex-body argument has additional substantive errors. Lemma 4.2 establishes uniformity of p(z_t) only as λ approaches zero, whereas Equation (43) uses exact uniformity at finite λ; boundary effects generally make this marginal nonuniform. Corollary 4.4 also omits the restriction to Lα distances with α≠2 introduced in Appendix E.2. Euclidean distances on a ball permit arbitrary orthogonal rotations, contradicting permutation-only identifiability as stated.

The proposed ICA justification does not follow from the spherical model. Coordinates of a uniformly distributed hyperspherical vector are dependent because their squared values sum to one, so the assumed independent sources required for linear ICA are incompatible with this distribution. The alternative argument using local isometry and PCA supplies neither sufficient conditions nor approximation bounds connecting the convex-body theorem to CLIP.

The experiments do not isolate disentanglement from ordinary preprocessing. FastICA changes dimensionality and performs whitening, but matched PCA-only and whitening-only baselines are absent. After whitening, an orthogonal ICA rotation leaves both dot products and the optimum of an L2-regularized linear classifier unchanged. Consequently, the reported improvements cannot establish that recovering independent components causes the gains.

The empirical identifiability claims exceed the measurements. Appendix K regresses learned representations on ground-truth latents; high R² in this direction can occur for a rank-deficient projection that loses latent factors. CelebA evidence consists of selected qualitative traversals without quantitative disentanglement metrics or controlled comparisons. Downstream classification gains likewise do not establish latent recovery.

The causal novelty is insufficiently established. The undirected edge specifies statistical dependence without defining intervention semantics or identifying causal effects. The joint distribution can still be factorized as p(z_x)p(z_t|z_x), and much of the identifiability machinery is explicitly inherited from Zimmermann et al. [67]. The paper needs a sharper account of what its causal formulation adds beyond a coupled latent-variable model.

Reproducibility and experimental uncertainty remain limited. Real-data results lack reported variability across seeds, and the data used to fit PCA/FastICA are unclear. This matters where requested dimensions exceed the few-shot sample count: EuroSAT uses 50 ICA components despite having only 10 support examples in the one-shot setting. The handling of this case and any additional fitting data must be specified.

strengths: The paper addresses an important question: what multimodal contrastive learning can recover when modalities contain related but nonidentical latent factors.
The empirical investigation is broad, including synthetic assumption violations, CelebA traversals, Multimodal3DIdent, and downstream evaluations across multiple CLIP encoders and datasets.

The proposed postprocessing is inexpensive and reports potentially useful improvements. For example, Table 2 increases ViT16 average target accuracy from 32.51% to 37.13%. The appendix provides several useful implementation details.
weaknesses: The central identifiability proofs depend on a false Lemma 2 (Appendix D.1). It claims that the normalized population loss has minimum zero. However, under the stated spherical model, the unit-circle case with k = tau = 1, cosine distance, and identity latent maps gives approximately -0.421. Furthermore, its required almost-sure equality between paired embeddings forces constant representations under the full-support noisy pairing distribution, contradicting the simultaneous requirement of uniform representations. Both Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 rely on this lemma, so their main guarantees are not established.

The convex-body proof has an additional substantive error: Equation (43) treats the target marginal as exactly uniform, whereas Lemma 3 establishes only a limit as lambda approaches zero. A truncated Laplace conditional on a bounded interval generally produces a nonuniform marginal at finite lambda because its normalization depends on location. Thus the stated exact symmetric cross-entropy reduction does not follow. Corollary 2 also omits the restriction to L-alpha distances with alpha different from 2 that appears in Appendix E.2; arbitrary norms do not guarantee permutation-only ambiguity.

The theoretical justification for FastICA is incompatible with the spherical assumptions. Cartesian coordinates of a uniformly distributed sphere are dependent, and the distribution is rotationally invariant. Consequently, ICA cannot identify preferred latent axes or resolve the orthogonal ambiguity under this model. The remark about having at most M-1 independent variables does not establish independent Cartesian sources. The proposed PCA/local-isometry argument likewise provides no guarantee transferring the convex-body result to CLIP.

The downstream experiments do not isolate disentanglement from whitening and dimensionality reduction. Appendix K compares ICA with 300 components against PCA-plus-ICA with 160 or 200 components, without matched PCA-only and whitening controls. An orthogonal ICA rotation of fixed whitened features leaves an L2-regularized linear probe unchanged. Therefore, these accuracy gains cannot establish that recovering independent components caused the improvement.

The direct recovery evaluations do not establish the claimed component-wise disentanglement in realistic settings. CelebA evidence is qualitative, and Multimodal3DIdent reports aggregate R-squared rather than component-wise recovery or independence. Additionally, Appendix K fits learned representations from ground-truth latents: high R-squared in this direction can hold for a rank-deficient representation and does not demonstrate recovery of every latent factor.

The 'beyond DAGs' contribution needs sharper justification. The undirected connection specifies statistical dependence without defining how heterogeneous causal mechanisms are represented or what causal conclusions follow. The paper does not establish why a model with an explicit latent regime variable is inadequate, and the experiments do not directly test the motivating mixture of opposing causal mechanisms. The geometric recovery arguments otherwise rely substantially on Zimmermann et al. (2021), making the correctness of the proposed multimodal extension especially important.

Experimental reporting leaves material uncertainty: downstream tables lack variability across seeds, and the data used to fit PCA/ICA and select component counts are insufficiently specified. Table 2 also reports the RN101 baseline target average as 20.03%, although its four entries average approximately 22.03%, exaggerating the corresponding improvement.
